I think people sail past each other's points on this issue constantly, so I'll try to cage it in as best as I can...

The point you seem to be making is that salvation must be determined solely by looking at the appearance of a man's works as "good deeds." But that missed some important points of what Christianity has to consider in this discussion. First, appearance is not reality. Good deeds on their face may not be so good if we really look into their motives. But, more importantly, salvation isn't strictly about our deeds. It's actually about the mercy of God.

If you want to be less theistic, you can say it's a personification of the idea that "reality forgives our errors" to some reasonable but very real extent. Certainly not egregious ones, but ones that are sufficiently surprising that we can find it notable. Therefore, while God certainly wishes us to do good works; or, less theistically, "reality works better for everyone when we're trying to be decent to others, those good works aren't actually earning the aforementioned "mercy." The ultimate objective of value in Christianity is that promise of mercy. Although we can and do err, we also rely on God to enable us to repent of our sins and overcome them.

The hypothetical virtuous man denying that "Jesus is lord" certainly can understand some actions are better than others. And these actions might be virtuous on their face. We call such an idea "civic righteousness" and it's a function of the truths inherent in God's Law that even unbelievers can understand. Even so, this is not a perfect metric and and every mistake is something which lacks a logical resolution without some kind of appeal to mercy. If such a person is relying on their "virtue" to get into heaven, they're going to be missing that promise of grace. And it is probable they will also lack an awareness of their own imperfections that can lead to such errors. Since you implied humility, it would presumably be that this person somehow assumes mercy exists without any discussion of the evidence.

But, no matter how much we look at his works and conclude that he's virtuous, it's still not going to generate the required mercy. From whence does he get that mercy? Himself? Not if you're relying on that virtue to get into heaven. Such a policy would be either ignorant or dishonest neither of which is truly virtuous. But, if it is built on a kind of trust, perhaps it is a seed of what God can cultivate into faith.

Conversely, the believer who speaks fondly of Jesus yet ignores what He stands for is also missing the point. Because at the end of the day this is not about you, but it's about what God does for us by grace. A hypocritical believer might know and speak of grace, but their assumption of their own perfection is what is dangerous to them. The beggar may not put themselves above their provider.

Thus, let me focus first on the words of Jesus: "Whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven." (Matthew 10:33) A simple reading is that merely denying Jesus is a cause for condemnation in and of itself. But obviously, this is a problem for our "kind unbeliever." Could a more sophisticated reading imply "denying what Jesus stands for?" Or, perhaps, that such a kind unbeliever should be led to eventually recognize what Christians really mean by Jesus?

By grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them. (Ephesians:2:8-10)

The entire point is really the same as that old "faith versus good works" debate. I must define the term faith accurately as I believe a certain monk from 500 years ago did. Faith is not merely an intellectual assent saying "I believe X." It also involves the integrity of putting one's trust in this. Those who live in ignorance of its origins may or may not yet have standing. But what is clear is that we really have no tools to gauge the ultimate state of such a thing in light of the current place.

The answer to "ye shall know them by their fruits" (Matthew 7:16) is not Pelagianism whereby "we save ourselves by our own choices." Indeed, a conversion to faith in Jesus cannot be coerced, but it is also something which the Holy Spirit works in, with, and under to bring us toward. This involves a "change of heart" caused by God, and that is the ultimate object of value. Saying "[hypothetical guy] is not a bad guy" is fine. But it really misses our key point. In Christianity we have a recognition and gratitude for God's hand working in everything.
